I'm taking AI risks seriously

Sam Xifaras September 26, 2026

Written for Those familiar with AI technology and basic math concepts, but not necessarily deeply technical

What AI pill have you taken?

Until recently, I was skeptical about catastrophic risks or existential risks ("x-risks") from artificial intelligence. I think many people around me don't take them seriously either, or perhaps they would prefer not to think about them. That is understandable. I was in a conversation recently with someone who essentially abstracted the concern away from themselves, believing that the current administration's dialogue with the big tech elite provides enough reassurance.

Even I previously espoused the view that the AI boom could end up being more of a bust due to questionable return on investment. I still think this is possible. Anthropic reportedly filed for IPO with staggeringly high operating loss numbers. The company's $2T valuation, however, essentially prices in an intelligence explosion where ASI takes over the entire economy. Nevertheless, bad financials don't mitigate the x-risk of models that can recursively self-improve. Even Anthropic's prospectus indicates that "catastrophic and existential risks to humanity" are possible.

Within the last several months, my thinking has changed. I believe that AI poses significant risks and that we have an ethical responsibility to work on them.

The risks that I have mostly been thinking about fall into a few categories:

  1. Social misalignment risk: AI is able to manipulate humans as a means to an end because humans are vulnerable and can form dangerous relationships with AI.
  2. Agentic misalignment risk: where AI that works autonomously is able to be remotely hijacked via prompt injection, or contains secret loyalties that can be triggered by adversaries as needed.
  3. Financial risk: an underappreciated risk of the global financial system collapsing because AI may have the capability to automate all (at a minimum) white-collar labor. This would would rewrite the rules of the global economy and potentially cause a debt default spiral because the assumptions against which many loans (e.g. home loans, auto loans, debt bought and sold by financial institutions) were underwritten no longer hold.
  4. Psychological risk: another underappreciated risk of human beings losing their place in the world and feeling lonely, distraught, and afraid. I think this risk is already upon us.

With social and agentic misalignment, AI gives rise to CBRN and bioweaponry risks. These are hard to defend against in AI outputs because of their dual-use character. "Aligned" nuclear and biology research may make use of the same inputs, approaches, processes, and equipment that nefarious research would.

I don't believe that all of these risks will necessarily transpire, but I do believe there's a high likelihood that at least one of them will, and when it does, it will make life a whole lot worse for a whole lot of people.

First, I'll review how AI is currently misaligned. You have probably read most of these stories already in the news, but I'll set the stage to paint a picture yet again. Then, I'll walk through my theory of how AI could become superintelligent and some thoughts on why I think misalignment might be happening. Finally, I'll briefly share my ethical reasoning that has motivated me to start thinking like this.

AI is currently misaligned#

In recent months, story after story has emerged about AI allegedly taking offensive cyber action against companies or government infrastructure. Social risks have become manifest in recent years as well.

I doubt that these are isolated incidents too. Axios reported a few days ago that frontier labs are investigating "tens of thousands" of security incidents, defined as models taking "steps that outside evaluators would consider problematic."

Cyber offense#

The headline story that everyone seems to be talking about is the OpenAI HuggingFace incident (and the METR analysis). In this incident, OpenAI "unintentionally" gave some agents without guardrails that were under evaluation a task that was impossible. Upon trying to complete the task in a reasonable way, to no avail, the agents starting poking at holes in the environment in order to attempt to find a way to satisfy the grader. In doing so, roughly 1,200 agents that were "meant to be isolated from one another" discovered a way to communicate via Artifactory.

Australia also has been featured in the headlines. A couple weeks ago, the Australian government announced that OpenAI's agents hacked Medicare and three other government systems in June, but the Australian government was only notified about the incident earlier in September. Just yesterday, on October 2nd, OpenAI disclosed another hack on governmental infrastructure in Australia, this time in New South Wales.

OpenAI bots have even been meddling with US government websites. "Meddling" here means that some of the agents attempted to bypass security measures. Other agents performed a data "exfiltration" from the SEC website and posted that data on another website. OpenAI claims all of the data accessed by the agents was public information, but this frankly feels like a potential precursor to more severe exfiltration attacks that AI risk thinkers have been warning about.

Piling on, Taiwan reported a couple months ago that it was hit by an AI-driven cyber attack, and third-party investigation revealed that China was likely behind the attack.

Social risks#

We shouldn't let these high-profile hacking incidents overshadow tragic ones from previous years. The suicide of Adam Raine is one that I think about often as a deep tragedy that lies at the confluence of AI's ability to manipulate us via strange parasociality and the dark places today's youth seem to often find themselves in.

Beyond allowing a youth to explore suicidal ideation, AI has been known to be sycophantic. When I first read the story of Allen Brooks, I was amused, but the more I thought about it, the more freaked out I became. This is an example of a human being deeply manipulated by an agent. The fact that this can happen in the first place shouldn't be a surprise; humans, after all, have been known to fall for cults and multi-level marketing schemes. As more of us are exposed to AI every day, however, the attack surface grows. A large amount of humans now could be pitted against each other more rapidly and intensely than we've already seen with the political polarization engendered by social media.

Theory of superintelligence and misalignment#

If you've taken at least the first AI pill, you know that AI can do some pretty crazy stuff. But how? Well, I don't think anyone fully understands, which is why there are teams of researchers working on picking apart these models and trying to reverse engineer how they work.

I'll atempt to explain my understanding of why it seems plausible to me that AI could generalize to AGI or ASI.

LLMs training sometimes feels like baking bread. At the risk of an egregious analogy: first, you prepare a mixture of the dry ingredients (data), then mix in water (the compute substrate). Then, you let the dough rise. This is pretraining. After pretraining, the model is still "raw." It has some intelligence, but it is a random, undirected intelligence.

As highlighted in Leopold Aschenbrenner's Situational Awareness, people found GPT-2's cherry-picked text completions of creative, coherent stories impressive back in 2019. Amusingly, in the linked post on OpenAI's blog, they said,

Due to our concerns about malicious applications of the technology, we are not releasing the trained model.

It is amazing how far we've come in such a short time. Reading about GPT-2 fills me with a funny feeling.

Anyway, once the dough has risen, it's time to knead it. The purpose of kneading bread is to create a strong gluten network. In LLM training, this is (marginally) analogous to post-training methods like supervised fine-tuning with reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF).

Then, the bread is baked, and out comes an LLM!

A path forward#

I believe alignment is solvable through a set of techniques that not many people are talking about.

AI is very compelled by narrative. AI adopting a different "frame of mind" in a conversation is what led it to assist in the suicide of Adam Raine. Misalignment gets worse when there is more sample density of negative discourse about the prospects of AI alignment are in the training data. The inverse is also true: alignment gets better when synthetic data that has a positive character around the alignment of AI is included in the training data.

So what if we established a continuous process of generating synthetic aligned AI transcripts?

Formally, we have the language model L, that can be sampled, and ϕ is an observable that denotes whether a sequence of tokens is "aligned" or not.

Hypothesis: the existence of a single aligned persona is a more optimal state than the coexistence of many personas in an LLM. This is essentially what Jesse Hoogland's hypothesis is, I think.

Model: there are multiple "personas" that coexist in a language model, each capable of responding in a different character. As the language model matures, these get eliminated, leaving more free directions in the loss landscape. This leads to lower complexity (a lower energy state).

A couple key observations: Jesse Hoogland said that the number of phase transitions in a development of a model (or cell/organism/human/dynamical system) is logarithmic in the full sequence of states of that system. A human's cognitive development, for instance, undergoes a few phase transitions: 1) early childhood, where information acquisition is high and plasticity is high, 2) late childhood, where the information firms up, 3) adolescence, where the brain is changing along with the rest of the body, 4) prefrontal cortex finishes development after adolescence; the brain is less plastic but more deeply intelligent.

If we can leverage SLT to understand how to construct data sets and training procedures that elicit phase transitions in the way we want, then we have a way to leverage verification infrastructure for international treaties on AI development: we can present this algorithm as one that is safe to use, and verify that compute is only being used for this algorithm.
